title: The libraries
hookLine: from Cordoba to Cairo to Timbuktu, great libraries

cards: A family in Timbuktu opens a wooden chest. Inside, wrapped in cloth and leather, are pages written by hand: prayers, law, astronomy, letters, poems, notes in the margins from readers long dead.
Families in that desert city kept papers like these for generations, and when they were threatened, people carried them away to safety. Why risk that much for old paper?
Because, to those families, a book was more than an object. In city after city across the Muslim world, people built rooms for books and opened their doors. Today: the libraries.

teach.b: Start with an oath. One surah of the Qur'an opens by swearing on writing itself. In Pickthall's translation: "By the pen and that which they write."
In Cordoba, in Muslim Spain, the court of the caliphs gathered a royal library, and chroniclers wrote of its size with open wonder.
In Cairo, the Fatimid rulers founded a house of knowledge, Dar al-Ilm, where people could come to read, copy and study.
In Timbuktu, the books lived not only in one great hall but in mosques, schools and family homes, passed down hand to hand. Three cities, three shapes of the same habit. What filled the shelves?
The Qur'an and its commentaries, law and hadith, yes. But also medicine, mathematics, grammar, poetry, geography, the stars.
Some collections were endowed through a waqf, like yesterday's soup kitchen, so the books stayed open to readers rather than locked away.
Some of these libraries burned, were scattered in wars, or were sold off page by page; some survive in pieces in archives around the world.

teach.h: BY THE PEN AND THAT WHICH THEY WRITE.
teach.b: What lasted longest was the expectation itself: that a city worth the name kept its books, and let people read them. A library in every city.

how: Muslims often treat books of religious learning with care, keeping copies of the Qur'an on a high shelf, and mosques often keep a small library for study and teaching.

games.q: your family in Timbuktu keeps a chest of old handwritten pages, and danger is coming to the city. what do you do?
o: leave the chest where it is and hope.
wrap the pages and carry them away to safety.
games.why: when the papers were threatened, people carried them away to safety, because a book was more than an object.

practice: Think of one thing you've always been curious about and never looked into: a place, a craft, a stretch of history, a question about the stars.
Picture the library shelf and the book that could answer it, kept by someone so a stranger could read it for free. If you pray, ask to learn something good; if not, just stay curious and breathe.

wordCard.voice: The libraries. From Cordoba to Cairo to Timbuktu, rooms of books, often endowed, kept open for readers. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the house of knowledge, the name of the Fatimid library and study house in Cairo.

carryVoice: Your line: a library in every city. Every open shelf was someone's gift to a stranger. That's today, done.
